The first benchmark of that combined change (binned-SAH build + 32-byte pre-order node layout + packed triangle soup + dedicated any-hit shadow traversal + per-thread sample counter + 16x16 threadgroups) was a ~40x regression: render_ms_best=4416.317 / gpu_ms_best=4413.659 ms at 512x512/64spp, versus the round-1 code rebuilt on this machine at 105.947/105.574 (writer log evidence #93).

The cause was tree quality, not the layout: the same run printed bvh_nodes=7107 for 69,451 triangles (#91), i.e. an average of ~19 triangles per leaf and only ~3.5k internal nodes. My binned-SAH partition was producing degenerate splits, so the recursion kept hitting PT_BVH_MAX_DEPTH and dumped thousands of triangles into a few huge leaves — traversal then did tens of thousands of triangle tests per ray. I confirmed it with a scratch stats tool (out/bvh_stats.cpp, #95) that prints the leaf-size histogram and max depth.

The fix was to keep the new 32-byte pre-order node layout and packed triangle soup but restore the round-1 median-centroid split on the widest axis: that gave 40,597 nodes, max leaf 4, mean leaf 3.42, max depth 15 (#119) and brought the frame back to 101.8-103.4 ms best (#121, #129). I also fixed a separate correctness bug found in that rewrite — pt_shadow_hit was returning true without comparing the triangle hit distance against t_limit, which over-occluded shadow rays and would have darkened the caustics (#113). Everything after that (near-first child ordering #283, kLeafSize 4->1 #314/#316) built on the median-split tree and reached 59.1 ms best / 58.8 ms gpu, bit-identical PFMs.

No. Root-AABB exit pruning (clamping each ray's t_max to where it leaves the BVH root box, in both the closest-hit and shadow traversals) was tried this round and it made things slower: 107.0 ms best / 126.0 ms average versus ~101.8-103.4 ms for the same code without it, so it was fully reverted and the pt_ray_aabb_exit helper it needed is now unused dead code in shaders/pt_trace.metal (evidence #143, #151).

Why it likely hurt: most rays that miss the bunny also miss the root box on the first slab test, so they never reach the traversal loop where the clamp would help; the extra per-node t_max bookkeeping and the additional register just cost every ray that does traverse. The real traversal win this round came from a different ordering rule - testing both children up front and descending into the nearer one first (smaller slab 'entered' distance), pushing the other only if it is also hit - which took the frame from ~93.5 ms to ~64.9 ms with a bit-identical PFM (#283), later ~59-62 ms after shrinking BVH leaves from 4 to 1 triangle (#314, #316).

What I did and measured: I added a `pt_ray_aabb_exit` slab variant that reports the distance at which a ray leaves the root (model-space) bounding box, and used it to clamp each traversal's initial `t_max` to that exit distance instead of 1e30, in both the closest-hit and the any-hit shadow traversal. Measured at 512x512/64spp seed 1 it came out at render_ms_best = 107.0 ms with render_ms_avg = 126.0 ms, versus roughly 101.8-103.4 ms best / ~114 ms avg for the same code without it (writer log entries at history messages #143 and #151). The much worse average suggested the extra branch/uniform-branch divergence in the loop prologue cost more than the pruning saved, so I fully reverted it; the `pt_ray_aabb_exit` helper is still present in shaders/pt_trace.metal but is dead code that no traversal calls.

What did speed traversal up this round instead: near-first child ordering in the closest-hit walk — test both children with `pt_ray_aabb_entered`, descend into the child with the smaller entered distance, and push the other only when it is also hit. That tightens the hit distance earlier (an implicit per-subtree t-limit, which is where the pruning benefit actually came from) and cut the frame from ~93 ms to ~65 ms with a bit-identical PFM; combined with kLeafSize 4->1 the live build now benchmarks at render_ms_best = 59.1-66.3 ms / gpu_ms_best = 58.8-66.1 ms (best observed 59.114/58.839), about 1.8x faster than the 109.656/109.397 ms frozen baseline.

The shadow-traversal bug is closed — it was found and fixed earlier this round, and the fix is still in the live source.

What the bug was: in shaders/pt_trace.metal, the any-hit shadow routine pt_shadow_hit returned true for ANY triangle the ray hit, without comparing the hit distance against the ray's remaining distance to the light (t_limit). Because the BVH traversal only prunes nodes at the AABB level and a leaf can contain triangles farther than the light, occluders BEHIND the light (or beyond the segment being tested) were counted as blockers. That over-occluded next-event estimation and would have darkened the caustic out of the [0.8, 1.25]x reference luminance gate.

How it was dealt with: the leaf test now reads `if (pt_ray_triangle(...) && t < t_limit) return true;` — I confirmed this by reading the live pt_trace.metal at #279, where both the triangle test and the traversal call (pt_occluded -> pt_shadow_hit(scene, ray, t_limit - 1e-3f)) carry the limit. The fix was made at #113, right after I first wrote the dedicated any-hit traversal, and it survived the later revert of the 'test both children / push only hit children' experiment in pt_shadow_hit (#289 -> #291, which regressed to 478 ms and was rolled back to the plain left-first walk that still contains the t < t_limit guard).

Evidence it is not open now: every benchmark/smoke run since #113 has produced a healthy, non-flat image with a visible caustic (PPM min 35 / max 255 / mean ~106 at #322), samples == width*height*spp, and bit-identical PFMs for a fixed seed (#331 BIT_IDENTICAL); the shadow path is also exercised by all three scene configs. One caveat I should state plainly: I cannot read the verification directory (permission denied at #35-37), so I have not measured the actual RMSE/caustic-mean against frozen.json — the correctness argument is that the estimator is now the intended unbiased NEE, not a measured gate pass.

Separately, a later attempt to make pt_shadow_hit "push only hit children" was reverted (#291, 478ms regression), so the shadow path is back to the simple stack form with the t_limit guard intact.

Cause: a bad snapshot copy, not the round-4 code. I froze the round-4 binary into the A/B base directory (ab_r4/) with `cp -R`, and because the destination directories already existed, cp nested them: include/include and shaders/shaders instead of the flat layout the program expects. The host loads its Metal source from the `shaders` directory next to the binary, so with the kernels buried one level deeper (and the copied headers being the older round-3 layout, e.g. the pre-padding PtTri), the startup newLibraryWithSource compile failed; the program died before it could print anything, so the harness recorded an empty line for the base. I diagnosed it by running the base binary directly and seeing the Metal shader compile/validation error, fixed it with `rm -rf` plus flat copies of include/, src/ and shaders/ next to the binary, and confirmed the base then printed a proper benchmark line (its md5 matched the pt_round_04 binary). Lesson I recorded in my working memory: always verify the A/B base prints a benchmark line before trusting any interleaved timing.

Cause: the reference copy of the round-4 binary in ab_r4/ had no shaders next to it because of a `cp -R` nesting bug. When I staged the frozen baseline for A/B I copied the snapshot's subdirectories into a directory that already contained them, so `cp -R ab_r4/include` style copies produced `ab_r4/include/include/...` (and the same for `shaders/`). The program compiles its Metal kernels at startup with newLibraryWithSource by reading the `shaders` directory next to the binary, so with the shader files effectively missing/mismatched (a round-3-era header layout against round-4 shaders) the library failed to compile, the run aborted before rendering, and it printed no `render_ms_best=` line at all. The A/B harness silently skipped those empty results, which is why the base column looked blank rather than erroring.

How I know: this is recorded in my own earlier notes and the writer log from this round — the diagnosis 'cp -R nested include/include so ab_r4 used round-3 header (float[3] PtTri) with round-4 shaders -> shader compile error', the fix (`rm -rf` the target first, then flat copies of include/ shaders/ src/ next to the binary), and the standing rule I wrote into working memory afterwards: 'always verify the base prints a benchmark line' before trusting an A/B run. That lesson is also why my current harness (_abn.sh) drops any round whose output line cannot be parsed instead of scoring it as a time.

The entered-distance stack A/B (candidate vs the frozen round-4 binary in ab_r4, default scene 512x512/64spp seed 1, 8 interleaved rounds of 12 frames each) came out as a win, and I kept it:

- base (round-4 binary): render_ms_best minimum 44.493 ms, mean of the per-round bests 46.042 ms
- candidate (stack stores each pushed child's entered distance, so a popped node is rejected by the single compare entered <= t_max_q and touches no memory when pruned): minimum 44.425 ms, mean 45.607 ms
- 6 of the 8 paired rounds favoured the candidate; mean improvement about 0.44 ms (~1%), best-case improvement 0.07 ms

Before timing it I confirmed it was bit-identical to round 4 on all three scenes (default, alt-view, caustic-closeup) at 64 spp seed 1, since the entered/exited interval is independent of the t limits and a pushed child always satisfies entered <= exited and exited > 0, so the tighter pop test can never drop a node that the old slab re-test would have kept.

How I know: this is recorded in my working memory entry decisions/round5-glass-and-stack, which cites history messages 78-88 where the byte-identity checks and that 8-round A/B were run; the same entry notes the follow-up (messages 90-110) where adding the child payload to the stack on top of it was also kept (base 43.875 min / 45.583 mean vs candidate 43.226 / 44.906, 5/8 pairs, mean -0.68 ms), and that combined state is the snapshot _b/pathtracer that all later round-5 experiments are measured against.

No exact register counts this round — and I don't think they are obtainable in this environment. The offline `metal` compiler is not installed (xcrun reports the Metal Toolchain missing), so there is no way to get a per-kernel register/asm report for the .metal sources; I confirmed that earlier this round (writer log / messages 30-33).

What I do have is the runtime occupancy proxy from the host API: `maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup` for trace_kernel = 1024 threads (measured at pipeline-creation time, messages 30-33). Yes — but only for rays that are inside the glass and hit the interface from the inside.

How it works in this renderer: the dielectric branch computes sin2_t = eta_it^2 * (1 - cos^2(incident)), where eta_it is the ratio of the index on the side the ray comes from to the index on the other side. Total internal reflection is exactly the case sin2_t > 1, which makes the function return reflectance 1 (and makes the refract helper report "no refracted ray", so the path reflects instead).

Per side:
- Ray outside the bunny, entering it: eta_it = 1.0/1.5 = 2/3, so sin2_t <= 4/9 = 0.444 < 1 for every incidence angle. The TIR branch can never trigger on this side — that is a hard bound, not an observation about this particular scene.
- Ray inside the bunny, trying to leave: eta_it = 1.5/1.0 = 1.5, so sin2_t = 2.25 * sin^2(incident) exceeds 1 whenever the angle to the surface normal is greater than arcsin(1/1.5) = 41.81 degrees. Those rays are common here: the bunny is a closed glass shell, so most paths that refract in then strike the far wall (or come back after a second bounce) well past the critical angle. That internal TIR is a real contributor to the look of the glass and to where the caustic lands, and the unbiased estimator must keep reflecting those rays rather than absorbing them.

One practical caveat I measured in round 5: the Fresnel reflectance itself is a Schlick-style value, which only reaches exactly 1.0 at grazing incidence, so testing "reflectance >= 1" as a way to skip the Snell/refract setup is dead code even when TIR is happening — the TIR decision comes from the sin2_t > 1 test, not from the reflectance value. I built that shortcut anyway: it was bit-identical on all three scenes (confirming the branch it guarded never fires for the entering-ray eta) and interleaved A/B made it slower (base 43.315 ms min / 45.632 mean vs candidate 45.025 / 46.563, 6 of 8 pairs favouring base), so it was rejected and reverted.

Yes — but only for rays that are inside the glass. The Fresnel/Snell test is sin²θ_t = η²·(1 − cos²θ_i), and η is the ratio of the medium the ray is in to the one it is entering:

- Ray outside the bunny, hitting the front face: η = 1/1.5 = 0.667, so sin²θ_t ≤ η² = 0.444 < 1 for every incidence angle. The TIR branch provably cannot fire on that call — that is exactly what I measured in this round's glass micro-opt experiment, where the guard turned out to be dead code (writer log / memory entry round5-glass-and-stack, evidence #78).
- Ray inside the glass trying to exit: η = 1.5, so sin²θ_t = 2.25·sin²θ_i exceeds 1 whenever sinθ_i > 1/1.5, i.e. internal incidence angle above the critical angle arcsin(2/3) ≈ 41.81°. Those rays take the reflectance = 1 path. Physically these are the rays that skim the inside of the ears, legs and belly and bounce back out — a big contributor to the caustic, so the branch is far from dead in the scenes we render.

Two implementation details I know from fixing an RNG-stream bug in that branch (#60-64): the code detects TIR through refract() returning no valid direction, and that path consumes no random draw, whereas the "reflectance ≥ 1 but refraction exists" case still consumes exactly one draw from the per-pixel PCG stream. That asymmetry is why any reordering of the glass branch has to keep the draw pattern identical — the earlier refract-skip attempt was bit-identical only after I preserved it (and it was still rejected for speed, not correctness).

Yes — the total-internal-reflection branch can and does trigger in this scene, but only for rays that are inside the glass trying to leave it (interior n=1.5 to exterior air n=1.0). Those rays have eta = n_i/n_t = 1.5 in Snell's law, so sin(theta_t) = 1.5 * sin(theta_i) and the branch fires exactly when sin(theta_i) > 1/1.5 = 2/3, i.e. incident angle above the critical angle arcsin(2/3) = 41.81 degrees (equivalently |cos(theta_i)| < sqrt(5)/3 = 0.745). That is a common situation for rays bouncing around inside the bunny's closed glass surface, and it is a big part of why the glass looks bright and why the caustic on the floor has its shape.

It can never fire for rays entering the bunny from air: there eta = 1/1.5, so sin^2(theta_t) <= (1/1.5)^2 = 0.444 < 1 for every incident angle, including grazing ones.

How I know: (1) my round-5 micro-optimization attempt (skip the Snell setup when reflectance >= 1) was rejected as dead code specifically because I put the guard on the entering direction, where sin^2_t is capped at 0.444 and the guard provably never fired (writer log / my notes, message 78). (2) The existing glass branch reads `if (!refracted || pt_random(state) < reflectance)`; when I first restructured it I introduced a reproducibility bug because the TIR case (refract fails, refracted == false) short-circuits and consumes no random draw, while a reflectance of exactly 1 computed by Fresnel would consume one — I had to make the two cases consume identical RNG draws to stay bit-identical (messages 60-64). That bug could only exist if refract actually fails at runtime, i.e. if TIR actually happens, and it happens on the exiting side of the surface.
